SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models

Shenli Zheng1, Zhou Fang1, Yuan Du1, Yijiang Liu2, Li Du1,∗ Affiliation: 1Nanjing University, Nanjing, China
2Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology, Nanjing, China
shenlizheng@smail.nju.edu.cn, zfang@nju.edu.cn
yuandu@nju.edu.cn, liuyijiang@nuist.edu.cn
∗Corresponding author: ldu@nju.edu.cn
Abstract

The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to π0.5\pi_{0.5}, SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a 1.98×\boldsymbol{1.98\times} full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.

With 0.09B LLM parameters (1.12B total), SPAR reaches 93.45% success after RL, an 8.90-percentage-point gain over its PAT-only counterpart.

I Introduction

Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT-2 [1], OpenVLA [2], and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [3] transfer pretrained representations to robotic manipulation, but their inference demands strain limited onboard compute. In π0.5\pi_{0.5}, the LLM accounts for 2.34B of 3.37B parameters. This motivates a central question: how much language-model capacity do manipulation tasks require, and how can a smaller policy retain useful capabilities?

Efficiency approaches include compact policies such as SmolVLA [4] and NORA [5], preference-based adaptation in NORA-1.5 [6], and synthetic pretraining in GraspVLA [7]. For existing policies, SP-VLA [8] and DART [9] reduce tokens, while EfficientVLA [10] and MoLe-VLA [11] reduce layer computation. Token reduction alone leaves backbone weights intact. EcoVLA [12] dynamically selects channels and attention heads; we instead permanently reduce backbone dimensions to produce a smaller dense model.

Permanent compression introduces a second challenge: recovering manipulation capabilities lost when parameters are removed. RLRC [13] combines structured pruning with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), while SimpleVLA-RL [14] demonstrates that interaction can improve policies beyond SFT. These results motivate studying how the allocation of a small parameter budget and adaptation during pruning affect subsequent recovery. The hidden dimension couples representations across Transformer blocks, whereas the intermediate dimension controls expansion within feed-forward layers. Their different roles motivate separate retention targets for the two dimensions.

We introduce SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which couples dimension-aware pruning with post-pruning RL to recover task performance (Fig. 2). Building on pruning-aware tuning (PAT) [15], SPAR jointly learns masks for the hidden and intermediate dimensions with separate retention targets and a regularized mask-learning objective. Channel selection and supervised adaptation are performed together, followed by physical pruning and fine-tuning of the reduced model. The resulting compact policy provides the initialization for RL, which further improves manipulation performance through interaction.

Our evaluation on LIBERO [16] and LIBERO-Plus [17] examines both task success and robustness under compression. Pruning only the intermediate dimension preserves high task success, while additional hidden-dimension pruning at a fixed intermediate-dimension retention target causes larger losses that RL can substantially mitigate. As a representative result, SPAR achieves 93.45% average LIBERO success with a 0.09B language backbone (1.12B total), approximately 4% of the original LLM size (). These findings support dimension-aware compression and recovery as complementary tools for compact robotic policies.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A dual-dimension pruning framework that jointly learns masks for the hidden and intermediate dimensions with separate retention targets and a regularized mask-learning objective.

  • •

    An empirical analysis of dimension sensitivity: pruning only the intermediate dimension preserves high task success, while additional hidden-dimension pruning causes larger performance losses in our evaluated tasks.

  • •

    An evaluation of recovery and efficiency across compression levels, showing improvements in task success and robustness after RL, together with measured full-policy inference acceleration.

II Related Work

II-A Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models

VLA models connect pretrained vision-language representations to robotic control. OpenVLA [2] predicts discretized actions autoregressively, whereas OpenVLA-OFT [18] uses parallel decoding and action chunking. CogACT [19] separates action generation into a diffusion expert. The π0\pi_{0} family [20] couples a PaliGemma backbone [21] with a flow-matching action expert; π0.5\pi_{0.5} [3] adds semantic subtask prediction. TinyVLA [22] instead combines a compact multimodal backbone with a diffusion decoder.

II-B Pruning for VLA models

LLM compression includes weight sparsification in SparseGPT [23], coupled-structure removal in LLM-Pruner [24], and row/column deletion to form smaller dense matrices in SliceGPT [25]. PAT [15] jointly performs hidden-dimension pruning and fine-tuning through trainable channel masks and Hybrid Sparsification Modules. For VLA models, DART [9] and SP-VLA [8] reduce visual tokens; EfficientVLA [10] removes low-impact layers, and MoLe-VLA [11] dynamically skips layers. EcoVLA [12] adaptively selects channels and attention heads with parallel sparsity updates and custom kernels. Building on PAT, SPAR learns masks for both the hidden and intermediate dimensions with separate retention targets, physically reduces the dense backbone, and applies RL recovery. Our evaluation examines the effects of compression on both manipulation success and robustness.

II-C Reinforcement learning for VLA models

RL for VLA models includes both offline and online approaches. Offline RL learns from a fixed dataset without additional environment interaction, whereas online RL collects new experience as training proceeds. The RECAP recipe for π0.6∗\pi_{0.6}^{*} [26] starts with offline RL pretraining, then alternates robot data collection with offline updates using advantage-conditioned policies. For online VLA training, SimpleVLA-RL [14] optimizes policies through environment interaction with outcome-based rewards, while RLinf [27] provides scalable training infrastructure. In the compression setting, RLRC [13] combines structured pruning, supervised fine-tuning, and RL to recover policy performance.

II-D Manipulation Benchmarks

LIBERO [16] evaluates knowledge transfer across language-conditioned manipulation tasks. ManiSkill2 [28] offers 20 task families spanning stationary and mobile manipulation, single- and dual-arm robots, and rigid and soft objects. Robustness-oriented extensions probe behavior beyond standard task completion: LIBERO-PRO [29] perturbs manipulated objects, initial states, instructions, and environments to examine sensitivity to memorized task conditions. LIBERO-Plus [17] evaluates seven perturbation dimensions, including camera viewpoints, robot initial states, and scene appearance. We use LIBERO to evaluate task success and LIBERO-Plus to assess robustness under perturbations after compression.

III Methodology

SPAR combines structural pruning with post-pruning RL (Fig. 2). We adapt pruning-aware tuning (PAT) [15] to jointly learn hidden and intermediate channel masks with separate retention targets. After mask learning, we physically remove inactive channels and finetune the compact policy before RL recovery. In our experiments, PAT only denotes this pruning and supervised adaptation stage within SPAR, and PAT+RL denotes the complete framework.

PAT background

PAT’s Hybrid Sparsification Module [15] combines channel selection with adaptation of pretrained weights. For a linear map 𝐖∈ℝdo×di\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{o}\times d_{i}}, its forward operation can be written as

𝐙=diag⁡(𝐌)​𝐃𝐖𝐗,\mathbf{Z}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{M})\mathbf{D}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}, (1)

where 𝐌\mathbf{M} selects output channels and 𝐃\mathbf{D} is the knowledge-transformation operator. The original formulation regularizes channel sparsity and the low-rank transformation’s orthogonality while optimizing the supervised objective. This joint optimization allows pretrained representations to adapt as channel selection changes. SPAR adopts the pruning-aware training principle and introduces separate retention targets for the hidden and intermediate dimensions, a sigmoid mask schedule, and a differentiable count penalty. The following subsections formulate these channel-selection components and their role in preparing the compact policy for recovery.

III-A Dual-Dimension Structural Pruning

The hidden dimension determines the width of the representation passed between Transformer blocks, whereas the intermediate dimension controls the expansion within each feed-forward network (FFN). Pruning the hidden dimension therefore requires coordinated changes to the attention and FFN projections to preserve residual connections. In contrast, pruning the intermediate dimension reduces the FFN expansion while leaving the residual-stream width unchanged. SPAR uses separate retention targets for the two dimensions to control these distinct aspects of model capacity.

Let dm​o​d​e​ld_{model} and df​f​nd_{ffn} denote the hidden dimension and the FFN intermediate dimension, respectively. We learn a mask for each dimension, 𝐌h​i​d∈[0,1]dm​o​d​e​l\mathbf{M}_{hid}\in[0,1]^{d_{model}} and 𝐌i​n​t∈[0,1]df​f​n\mathbf{M}_{int}\in[0,1]^{d_{ffn}}, with retention targets ρh​i​d\rho_{hid} and ρi​n​t\rho_{int}. Both masks are shared across layers. Writing their diagonal forms as 𝐃h=diag⁡(𝐌h​i​d)\mathbf{D}_{h}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{M}_{hid}) and 𝐃i=diag⁡(𝐌i​n​t)\mathbf{D}_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{M}_{int}), we apply the hidden-dimension mask to the attention projections:

𝐖{Q,K,V}′\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{\{Q,K,V\}} =𝐖{Q,K,V}​𝐃h,\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{\{Q,K,V\}}\mathbf{D}_{h}, (2)
𝐖O′\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{O} =𝐃h​𝐖O.\displaystyle=\mathbf{D}_{h}\mathbf{W}_{O}.

The FFN projections depend on both dimensions and are masked as

𝐖{u​p,g​a​t​e}′\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{\{up,gate\}} =𝐃i​𝐖{u​p,g​a​t​e}​𝐃h,\displaystyle=\mathbf{D}_{i}\mathbf{W}_{\{up,gate\}}\mathbf{D}_{h}, (3)
𝐖d​o​w​n′\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\prime}_{down} =𝐃h​𝐖d​o​w​n​𝐃i.\displaystyle=\mathbf{D}_{h}\mathbf{W}_{down}\mathbf{D}_{i}.

In 𝐖u​p\mathbf{W}_{up} and 𝐖g​a​t​e\mathbf{W}_{gate}, rows correspond to the intermediate dimension and columns to the hidden dimension; this arrangement is reversed in 𝐖d​o​w​n\mathbf{W}_{down}. Sharing the hidden-dimension mask across blocks ensures that their residual connections use the same retained channels. Once the masks are binarized, we remove the rows and columns associated with inactive channels. The resulting backbone uses smaller dense weight matrices while preserving the visual-token sequence and Transformer depth.

III-B Mask Learning and Regularization

At low retention, mask learning must select a small set of channels while preserving task-relevant representations. We combine continuous gates for gradient-based adaptation, a count penalty for the retention target, and binary regularizers for decisive channel selection. This formulation allows the supervised objective to guide channel importance while progressively preparing the masks for physical pruning.

Soft-to-hard masking

For either mask, trainable mask logits 𝐖M\mathbf{W}_{M} are initialized to +1.5+1.5 for an initial candidate set of retained channels and −1.5-1.5 for the remaining channels. These assignments remain learnable during supervised adaptation. During training,

𝐌⁡(s)=σ⁡(τ⁡(s)​𝐖M),\mathbf{M}(s)=\sigma\!\left(\tau(s)\mathbf{W}_{M}\right), (4)

where σ\sigma is the logistic sigmoid and ss is the training step. The inverse temperature increases linearly from 1 to 10:

τ⁡(s)=1+9​min⁡(srs​t​o​p​s0,1),\tau(s)=1+9\min\!\left(\frac{s}{r_{stop}s_{0}},1\right), (5)

where s0s_{0} is the reference training horizon for the schedule and rs​t​o​pr_{stop} controls its endpoint (typically 0.8). The inverse temperature reaches 10 at step rs​t​o​p​s0r_{stop}s_{0}, progressively sharpening the mask toward binary values. After mask learning, we set 𝐌b​i​n=𝟙[𝐖M≥0]\mathbf{M}_{bin}=\mathds{1}[\mathbf{W}_{M}\geq 0] and use the resulting channel selection for physical pruning.

The gate’s derivative makes the optimization trade-off explicit:

∂Mj∂WM,j=τ⁡(s)​Mj​(1−Mj).\frac{\partial M_{j}}{\partial W_{M,j}}=\tau(s)M_{j}(1-M_{j}). (6)

The supervised loss updates channel selection through these gradients, with larger responses near the decision boundary and smaller responses near the binary endpoints. Annealing progressively sharpens the masks as the policy adapts. Once the masks are thresholded, the retained channel set is fixed and supervised fine-tuning adapts the reduced dense matrices to the manipulation tasks.

Pruning objective

We use three regularizers to encourage target retention and binary channel selection. For a mask with dd entries and target active-channel count Nt​a​r​g​e​tN_{target}, the count penalty is

ℒc​o​u​n​t=λ1​(∑j=1dMj−Nt​a​r​g​e​tNt​a​r​g​e​t)2.\mathcal{L}_{count}=\lambda_{1}\left(\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{d}M_{j}-N_{target}}{N_{target}}\right)^{2}. (7)

The soft count ∑jMj\sum_{j}M_{j} replaces a hard active-channel count during optimization. Its derivative with respect to any mask entry is

∂ℒc​o​u​n​t∂Mj=2​λ1Nt​a​r​g​e​t2​(∑k=1dMk−Nt​a​r​g​e​t).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{count}}{\partial M_{j}}=\frac{2\lambda_{1}}{N_{target}^{2}}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{d}M_{k}-N_{target}\right). (8)

Thus, a count above the target encourages smaller mask values, and a count below it encourages larger values. The supervised loss guides the selection of individual channels, while this penalty encourages the aggregate soft count to approach the target. To promote near-binary channel assignments, we add entropy regularization:

ℒe​n​t​r​o​p​y=−λ2∑j=1d[Mj​ln⁡(Mj+ϵ)+(1−Mj)ln(1−Mj+ϵ)],\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{entropy}=-\lambda_{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\big[&M_{j}\ln(M_{j}+\epsilon)\\ &+(1-M_{j})\ln(1-M_{j}+\epsilon)\big],\end{split} (9)

The discreteness term further encourages separation from the threshold at 0.5:

ℒd​i​s​c=λ3​(0.5−∑j=1d|Mj−0.5|),\mathcal{L}_{disc}=\lambda_{3}\left(0.5-\sum_{j=1}^{d}|M_{j}-0.5|\right), (10)

where λ1\lambda_{1}, λ2\lambda_{2}, and λ3\lambda_{3} weight the terms and ϵ=10−7\epsilon=10^{-7} stabilizes the logarithms. The training objective combines these penalties with the supervised policy fine-tuning loss ℒS​F​T\mathcal{L}_{SFT}:

ℒt​o​t​a​l=ℒS​F​T+ℒc​o​u​n​t+ℒe​n​t​r​o​p​y+ℒd​i​s​c.\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{SFT}&+\mathcal{L}_{count}\\ &+\mathcal{L}_{entropy}+\mathcal{L}_{disc}.\end{split} (11)

Together, these soft penalties encourage near-binary masks with soft counts close to the target channel budgets, while the supervised loss guides task-relevant channel selection. We then binarize the masks, physically remove inactive channels, and continue supervised fine-tuning of the pruned model. Table VI evaluates each regularizer when pruning only the intermediate dimension.

Mask-budget convergence

Fig. 3 shows π0.5\pi_{0.5} mask learning on LIBERO at 10% hidden and intermediate retention targets. Both soft counts are within 0.05% of their aligned targets by step 3000.

III-C Post-Pruning RL Recovery

After mask learning, physical pruning, and supervised fine-tuning, the compact policy may still exhibit reduced task success. We therefore use RL to improve manipulation behavior through simulated interaction, building on the representations retained during compression.

We use Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [30] with RLinf [27] for parallel simulation rollouts and distributed policy updates. A sparse binary reward assigns 1 to successful task completion and 0 otherwise, providing a direct training signal without task-specific dense reward shaping. Rewards and log-probabilities are aggregated at the action-chunk level. PPO maximizes the clipped policy surrogate

Jc​l​i​p(θ)=𝔼t[min(rt​(θ)​A^t,clip(rt(θ),1−δ,1+δ)A^t)],\begin{split}J_{clip}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\min\big(&r_{t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{t},\\ &\operatorname{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\delta,1+\delta)\hat{A}_{t}\big)\big],\end{split} (12)

where sts_{t} is the policy’s multimodal observation, ata_{t} is an action chunk, and rt​(θ)=πθ​(at∣st)/πθo​l​d​(at∣st)r_{t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})/\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) compares its probability under the current and rollout policies. The normalized generalized advantage estimate A^t\hat{A}_{t} guides the policy update, while δ\delta controls the clipping range. Using task-completion feedback, the actor–critic loss trains the action expert and value head while keeping the pruned backbone frozen. The architecture remains fixed; paired evaluations before and after RL measure improvement over PAT only.

IV Experiments

Tasks and Training Protocol

We train one policy per configuration across all 40 tasks in LIBERO’s Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long (LIBERO-10) suites [16], covering spatial, object, goal, and long-horizon variation. Using OpenPI’s PyTorch π0.5\pi_{0.5} implementation [31] with a Gemma 2B backbone, we vary retention targets for the hidden and intermediate dimensions and report suite success rates and their mean.

Baselines

We compare with unpruned π0.5\pi_{0.5} before and after RL and published results for NORA [5], NORA-1.5 [6], SmolVLA [4], GraspVLA [7], and EcoVLA [12]. SPAR’s parameter-pruning ratios are relative to the unpruned full model (3.37B) and LLM (2.34B), with pruning percentages rounded to integers. EcoVLA’s labels denote its reported channel/head pruning settings.

Implementation Details

SFT uses a batch size of 256 for 30,000 steps: 6,000 for PAT mask learning and 24,000 for post-pruning fine-tuning. Training and RL use NVIDIA A800 GPUs. We deploy on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and measure median full-policy inference latency using TensorRT.

PPO Configuration

PPO uses eight NVIDIA A800 GPUs on one node, with 128 training and 80 evaluation environments across all four suites. The actor global batch size is 2,048, with a per-rank micro-batch size of 128 and two gradient-accumulation steps. The runner allows up to 200 RL epochs.

IV-A Main Results

Pruning only the intermediate dimension preserves high task success (Table I). A 10% intermediate-dimension retention target reduces the LLM from 2.34B to 0.82B with 96.45% average success, only 0.35 percentage points below the baseline’s 96.80%. This suggests substantial FFN intermediate-dimension redundancy on these tasks, motivating ρi​n​t=0.1\rho_{int}=0.1 for subsequent experiments.

Additional hidden-dimension pruning causes larger losses (Table II): reducing ρh​i​d\rho_{hid} from 0.9 to 0.1 lowers average success without RL from 95.90% to 84.55%, most sharply on Long. RL substantially mitigates these losses, improving all five pruned averages by 1.90–8.90 percentage points versus 0.90 for the baseline. Notably, at ρh​i​d=0.7\rho_{hid}=0.7 and ρi​n​t=0.1\rho_{int}=0.1, RL achieves 97.55%, just 0.15 points below the unpruned RL baseline’s 97.70%, with approximately 52% fewer total and 75% fewer LLM parameters. Even the smallest policy (1.12B total / 0.09B LLM) improves from 84.55% to 93.45%, recovering much of the loss while remaining 4.25 points below that baseline.

IV-B Robustness on LIBERO-Plus

LIBERO-Plus [17] tests changes in camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, lighting, background textures, sensor noise, and object layouts. Table III reports cross-suite scores by perturbation category and the aggregate score under Overall.

RL substantially improves all five pruned overall scores by 5.52–9.35 percentage points, versus 0.47 for the baseline. The smallest policy improves from 47.46% to 56.81% but remains 27.64 points below the unpruned RL baseline, particularly under robot-initial-state and language perturbations. Even at ρh​i​d=0.9\rho_{hid}=0.9 and ρi​n​t=0.1\rho_{int}=0.1, the recovered policy scores 78.20% versus the baseline’s 84.45%. This 6.25-point gap, despite nearly matched standard LIBERO performance, indicates greater sensitivity to perturbations after compression. Robustness-critical applications may therefore require less aggressive pruning or further RL adaptation with broader perturbation exposure.

IV-C Real-Robot Evaluation

On an AgileX dual-arm platform, we evaluate six tasks with 20 trials each (Table IV); Fig. 4 illustrates Task 5. Pruning only the intermediate dimension with ρi​n​t=0.2\rho_{int}=0.2 yields 2.02B total / 0.99B LLM parameters, approximately 40% / 58% fewer than the baseline. The compact policy retains much of the baseline’s manipulation performance: 76/120 successes (63.33%) versus 85/120 (70.83%), a 7.50-percentage-point decrease. It matches the baseline on Task 1 and records successes on all six tasks. These results show that intermediate-dimension pruning preserves practical manipulation capability on physical hardware despite substantial parameter reduction.

IV-D Inference Latency

Table V reports full-policy latency and memory on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. At 10% intermediate retention, latency falls from 295.04 ms to 170.64 ms (1.73×\times); adding hidden-dimension pruning at the same retention reaches 148.71 ms, a 1.98×1.98\times speedup and 49.60% latency reduction. GPU memory decreases from 7.098 to 2.627 GiB, approximately 63% lower than the baseline.

IV-E Ablation Study

Table VI shows that the full objective in Table I achieves the highest average success rate. Removing the count, entropy, or discreteness term lowers the average by 0.75, 0.35, or 0.40 percentage points, respectively. The full objective also achieves the highest Long-suite score, supporting the combined use of budget and binarization penalties in this configuration.

V Limitations and Future Work

Although SPAR approaches or slightly exceeds the unpruned RL baseline on LIBERO under some aggressive compression settings, a robustness gap remains on LIBERO-Plus. Evaluation is also limited to one backbone and one intermediate-dimension pruning configuration across six real-robot tasks, motivating broader backbone studies, joint hidden-dimension and intermediate-dimension pruning on robots, and energy measurements across deployment platforms.

To further improve recovery, we envision using SimFoundry [32] to reconstruct real-world AgileX task scenes as simulation environments. TiPToP [33] and ASPIRE [34] could then generate trajectories through planning and program execution, with MimicGen [35] expanding their coverage for supervised adaptation of compact policies. Building on this initialization, the policies would undergo online reinforcement learning with PPO through direct interaction in the real-to-sim environments reconstructed by SimFoundry.

VI Conclusion

SPAR jointly prunes the hidden dimension and intermediate dimension with separate retention targets, combining pruning-aware adaptation with PPO-based recovery. Intermediate-only pruning preserves high success, while RL partially restores hidden-dimension losses. With a 0.09B LLM and 1.12B total parameters, the compact policy achieves a 1.98×1.98\times inference speedup, while RL raises its LIBERO success from 84.55% to 93.45%. On AgileX, 20% intermediate retention leaves a 7.50-point gap to the baseline. These results support combining dimension-aware compression and RL to improve the performance–size trade-off of VLA models.
